prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We have gone out in boats upon the sea at night, lost, and the vast waters close traps of fear about us. The boats are driven apart, and we are alone at last under the incalculable sky, listless, diseased with stars. Let the oars be idle, my love, and forget at this time our love like a knife between us defining the boundaries that we can never cross nor destroy as we drift into the heart of our dream, cutting the silence, slyly, the bitter rain in our mouths and the dark wound closed in behind us. Forget depth-bombs, death and promises we made, gardens laid waste, and, over the wastelands westward, the rooms where we had come together bombd. But even as we leave, your love turns back. I feel your absence like the ringing of bells silenced. And salt over your eyes and the scales of salt between us. Now, you pass with ease into the destructive world. There is a dry crash of cement. The light fails, falls into the ruins of cities upon the distant shore and within the indestructible night I am alone.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker describes being lost at sea at night, surrounded by fear and isolation.
- The drifting boats symbolize separation, loneliness, and an inability to bridge emotional distance.
- The speaker urges their lover to forget love, war, death, broken promises, and destroyed places.
- Even while leaving, the lover’s absence remains painfully present to the speaker.

prompts.L4:

The text explores fear, isolation, and fractured love amid warlike destruction through a surreal nocturnal sea voyage filled with images of drifting boats, ruins, salt, and silence. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Let, Forget

outputs.L1:
We have gone out in boats upon the sea at night, lost, while the vast waters close traps of fear around us. The boats are driven apart, and at last we are alone beneath the incalculable sky, listless, diseased with stars. Let the oars be idle, my love, and, in this moment, let us forget our love—like a knife between us, defining the boundaries we can never cross nor destroy—as we drift into the heart of our dream, cutting the silence slyly, with bitter rain in our mouths and the dark wound closing behind us.

Forget the depth-bombs, death, and the promises we made; forget the gardens laid waste and, over the westward wastelands, the rooms where we had come together, bombed. But even as we leave, your love turns back. I feel your absence like the ringing of bells now silenced, and the salt over your eyes, and the scales of salt between us.

Now you pass with ease into the destructive world. There is a dry crash of cement. The light fails, falling into the ruins of cities upon the distant shore, and within the indestructible night, I am alone.
outputs.L2:
At night we have taken boats out onto the ocean, adrift and without direction, while the immense water gathers around us like snares made of fear. The boats are forced away from one another, until finally we are separate beneath a sky too vast to measure, emptied of will, sickened by the stars.

Leave the oars unmoving, my love, and for now put aside our love—that blade between us, marking limits we can neither cross nor break—as we float deeper into the center of our dream. We move through the silence, quietly cutting it open, with harsh rain on our tongues and the black wound sealed behind us.

Forget the depth charges, the dead, the vows we gave each other, the ruined gardens, and, farther west beyond the wastelands, the bombed rooms where we once met. Yet even while we go away, your love looks back. I sense your absence like bells whose ringing has suddenly been stopped. Salt lies over your eyes, and salt forms its hard scales between us.

Now you slip easily into the world of destruction. Cement breaks with a dry, sharp sound. The light weakens and drops into the wreckage of cities along the far shore, and inside the unbreakable night, I remain by myself.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who feels lost and abandoned, as if adrift at sea in the middle of the night. This setting creates an atmosphere of fear, uncertainty, and isolation. The darkness of the sea reflects the speaker’s emotional state: they are surrounded by loneliness and unable to find safety, direction, or comfort. The night becomes more than a physical setting; it represents confusion, grief, and the frightening experience of being emotionally alone.

The image of drifting boats deepens this sense of separation. Boats normally suggest movement or connection across water, but here they appear to drift apart, unable to reach one another. They symbolize loneliness and the emotional distance between the speaker and their lover. No matter how close they may once have been, they are now separated by a space that cannot be crossed. The boats suggest that love has become fragile and directionless, carried away by forces beyond the speaker’s control.

The speaker also urges their lover to forget many painful things: love, war, death, broken promises, and destroyed places. This repeated call to forget suggests a desire to escape suffering and memory. Love is placed alongside violence and ruin, implying that it too has become associated with pain. The speaker seems to understand that memory can keep wounds open, and so they ask the lover to let go of everything that has caused grief. However, the request also feels impossible, because the very act of naming these things shows how deeply they remain in the speaker’s mind.

Even as the lover leaves, their absence continues to dominate the speaker’s world. The lover is physically gone, yet emotionally they remain painfully present. This creates a powerful contradiction: departure does not bring freedom or closure, but instead makes the speaker more aware of what has been lost. The absence becomes almost tangible, filling the space around the speaker and intensifying their solitude.

By the end of the poem, the imagery grows darker and more devastated. Ruined cities, fading light, and the approach of darkness suggest a world marked by destruction and loss. These images connect personal heartbreak with broader scenes of war and collapse, making the speaker’s loneliness feel vast and inescapable. The failing light implies that hope is disappearing, leaving the speaker alone among memories, ruins, and silence. The poem closes with a profound sense of solitude, showing how love, once lost, can leave behind an inner landscape as desolate as a destroyed city or a dark sea.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a dark and dreamlike meditation on fear, isolation, and damaged love in a world marked by warlike destruction. Its central movement unfolds as a nocturnal sea voyage, but this voyage is less a realistic journey than a surreal passage through devastation. Boats drift through darkness, ruins appear like remnants of a shattered civilization, and the repeated presence of salt, water, silence, and night creates an atmosphere of abandonment. The sea becomes a space where memory, grief, and historical violence merge. It carries the speaker away, yet it also surrounds them with signs of loss, as if there is no escape from the ruined world they are trying to cross.

Throughout the text, love is presented as fragile and divided. It does not offer safety or rescue; instead, it is pulled apart by fear and by the pressure of catastrophe. The beloved is associated with distance, disappearance, and return, suggesting that intimacy cannot remain untouched by the destruction around it. Love turns back toward the devastated world, toward suffering and obligation, and this turning makes separation inevitable. The speaker’s personal grief is therefore not merely private. Their loss reflects a wider collective ruin, in which human bonds are broken by violence, exile, and historical disaster.

The imagery of silence deepens this sense of isolation. The world seems emptied of ordinary voices and meanings. What remains are fragments: drifting vessels, broken landscapes, salt-covered traces, and the oppressive darkness of night. These images suggest both physical destruction and emotional desolation. The speaker moves through a space where everything familiar has been dissolved or made strange. Even love, which might have promised connection, becomes another sign of fracture.

By the end, the text leaves the speaker alone in an “indestructible night.” This night is not simply the absence of light; it represents a condition that cannot be easily overcome. It is the persistence of fear, memory, and ruin after the possibility of reunion has vanished. The final loneliness is both intimate and historical. The speaker’s abandonment mirrors the larger abandonment of a world devastated by war. In this way, the text transforms a personal experience of separation into a broader vision of collective catastrophe, showing how love and loss are inseparable from the broken world that surrounds them.
outputs.L5:
**The Letting Go of Forgetting**

The mind has a strange way of holding on to what we wish it would release, while letting slip the things we try hardest to remember. We tell ourselves, “Let it go,” but the heart does not always follow instructions. Some memories stay like echoes in an empty room, returning when everything is quiet.

To forget is not always a failure. Sometimes it is a kindness. We forget small pains, old embarrassments, and words that once felt heavy. In time, even sharp memories can become softer, less like wounds and more like lessons.

The important thing is not to force ourselves to forget, but to let life continue. Let new days arrive. Let new thoughts grow. Let the past become part of the story, not the whole story.

And perhaps that is the quiet wisdom of healing: not to erase what happened, but to remember without being trapped by it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark surrealist prose poem about two lovers separated in boats at night during wartime, with imagery of the sea, ruins, bombs, salt, and loneliness.
counterfactuals.output:
At night the sea put on its black uniform and carried them away from each other.

Two boats, no larger than thoughts, drifted between the teeth of the harbor. In one, she sat with her hands folded around a lantern that had forgotten how to burn. In the other, he listened to the oars knock softly against the hull, like bones asking to be let back into the body.

Behind them, the city was practicing how to disappear.

Bombs opened their red flowers among the roofs. Churches knelt without meaning to. Windows leapt from their frames and became brief, glittering birds before the water swallowed them. The streets, where they had once walked with bread under one arm and the future under the other, lay broken in pale strips, salted with plaster, ash, and the dust of names.

He could see her only when the explosions lifted the dark.

Each burst of fire painted her face for an instant: the cheek he had kissed beside the fish market, the mouth that had once spoken his name as if it were a cup of warm milk, the eyes now wide and maritime, already belonging partly to the drowned.

Then darkness closed again, and she became a rumor in a boat.

The sea moved between them with the patience of an executioner. It smelled of salt, oil, and iron. Dead fish shone belly-up like small moons. Somewhere a mast burned. Somewhere a horse screamed from a square that no longer existed. The water carried pieces of their city past them: a door without a house, a doll’s arm, a prayer book swollen to twice its faith.

She wanted to call to him, but her voice had been requisitioned by the war. All she could do was open her mouth and release a flock of black gulls. They flew in circles above the boats, crying his name in languages neither of them had learned.

He reached toward her.

His arm lengthened impossibly over the water, pale and thin as a bridge made of candle wax. But the waves rose up wearing soldiers’ helmets and bit it back. He held the stump against his chest and laughed, because grief had finally become ridiculous. Because love, in wartime, was a room with no floor.

The bombs fell closer.

The sky shook out its pockets: fire, nails, the teeth of children, burning maps. The ruins answered with their own low music. Every stone in the city remembered being touched. Every staircase remembered feet. Every bed remembered sleep and punished the living for losing it.

Between the boats, loneliness stood upright on the water.

It was taller than the lighthouse and faceless, dressed in a coat sewn from wet flags. It leaned down and whispered first to her, then to him, telling each the other had already vanished. But still they saw one another in the intermittent wounds of light.

She lifted the dead lantern.

He lifted his empty hand.

For a moment, the sea became glass, and beneath it they saw the drowned future waiting: a kitchen with blue tiles, a child’s red shoe by the door, two cups on a table, apricots in a bowl, morning arriving without sirens. Then the vision cracked under the weight of artillery, and the future sank, turning slowly, like a ship with no passengers.

Salt gathered on their lips.

Not from kisses. Not from tears. From the sea climbing patiently into them, making them preservable, making them relics. By dawn, perhaps, they would be found far apart on opposite shores, white with salt, beautiful and useless as saints in abandoned chapels.

But night had not finished with them.

The boats continued outward, each pulled by an invisible tide, each carrying half of a single heart. The city burned behind them like a memory trying to keep warm. Above, the stars hid their faces. Below, the sea repeated its one dark sentence against the wood:

Apart, apart, apart.

And still, across the black water, through smoke and ruin and the falling iron of nations, they loved—  
not as the living love, with doors and bread and morning—  
but as two shipwrecks dream of shore,  
as salt dreams of the wound,  
as the last light dreams, terribly, of being seen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a modernist, melancholy passage in the voice of a lost sailor addressing their lover, blending romance, fear, and the destruction of cities.
counterfactuals.output:
My love, if this reaches you, it will arrive smelling of salt and smoke.

All night the sea has been lifting its black shoulders under the boat, and I have spoken your name into the wind until it came back to me broken, as if the dark itself had teeth. There are no stars. There is only the compass shivering like a frightened animal, the wet rope, the groan of timber, and somewhere beyond the rim of rain, the red pulse of cities dying.

I saw them from the water.

First the harbor went—its cranes bowing like metal saints, its warehouses opening in blossoms of fire. Then the avenues, those bright veins where we once walked with our hands hidden in one coat pocket, filled with ash. Towers leaned into one another as if for comfort. Windows burst outward by the thousand, a glittering weather, and the bells—do you remember the bells?—rang without hands, without hours, until the steeples fell and the sound became only dust.

I was afraid then, but not of death. Death is too simple a country. I was afraid of forgetting the exact warmth of your face when you slept, the small crease between your brows, the way you said my name as though it were something saved from a wreck. I was afraid the world would end and take from me not my body, but the proof that I had once been loved.

The men are gone now. One by one the sea has collected them, quietly, almost politely. I remain, a splinter of intention, drifting among the ruins of maps. The waves slap the hull like impatient hands. Beneath me, the drowned city repeats itself in broken light: domes, chimneys, the pale ribs of bridges, all wavering as if memory were water and water were guilt.

If morning comes, I will turn toward any coast that still believes in land. If it does not, know this: in the last kingdom of fear, I kept you with me. Not as a picture, not as a prayer, but as the secret architecture by which I did not collapse. The cities burned; the sea rose; the names of nations loosened and sank.

But your name, my love—your name stayed afloat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense lyrical paragraph that feels like a wartime dream: lovers adrift on the ocean, drifting apart beneath the stars, with bombed rooms and ruined shores in the distance.
counterfactuals.output: At night the sea carried them like a torn letter, two lovers loosened from the same sentence, their hands briefly touching over the black water before the tide revised them apart. Above, the stars burned with the cold patience of signal lamps, and below, the ocean breathed in its sleep, swelling with the murmur of drowned cities and names no one would answer to again. Far behind them, the shore lay open and ruined, its cliffs powdered with ash, its houses broken into roofless rooms where curtains still lifted in the wind like pale surrender flags, where a bed, split by shrapnel, held the moonlight in place of bodies. Somewhere guns continued their iron coughing, softened by distance until they sounded almost like thunder in a dream, almost like a heart refusing to stop. She drifted east, he west, each raft a fragment of the other’s memory, each wave widening the black seam between them, while constellations leaned down as if to witness or absolve. In the bombed rooms of the coast, rain filled teacups, flowers grew through floorboards, and mirrors kept flashing with the faces they had been before the war taught the world to burn. Still they called to one another across the glittering waste, their voices unraveling into salt and wind, and the sea, vast, indifferent, merciful only in its music, rocked them farther beneath the stars, toward separate dawns that smelled of smoke, roses, and nothing saved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an apocalyptic love prose-poem using long sentences, nautical imagery, and themes of absence, memory, and emotional devastation.
counterfactuals.output:
When the last sirens drowned beneath the harbor and the moon lowered itself like a dead lantern into the oil-black sea, I stood on the ruined quay with your name filling my mouth like saltwater, unable to speak it without swallowing the whole catastrophe again, and all around me the city leaned into its own disappearance, its towers cracked like masts after a storm, its windows glittering with the cold intelligence of stars that had already decided to abandon us.

You were not there, which was the shape the world had learned to take after you left: a room without a door, a ship without a compass, a shoreline erased by fog before the sailor has finished praying for it, and I, who had once believed love was an anchor, discovered too late that it was also the chain, the depth, the wreck, the immense pressure of everything unsaid closing over the ribs.

I remembered your hands most clearly at the end, not your voice, though your voice had once moved through me like a tide through moonlit caves, but your hands—those small pale vessels of mercy—lifting a cup, fastening a button, touching my face as if I were something still worth saving, while beyond the curtains the weather of history gathered itself into a single black wave.

Now every street is a canal of ash, every church bell a buoy tolling for the drowned, every gull a white scrap of a letter the sea refuses to deliver, and I walk through the wreckage with the terrible patience of one who has survived the end of the world only to find that survival is not an island but an ocean, and that memory is the cruelest captain, steering always toward the place where the beloved vanished.

I have kept, in the flooded hold of my heart, the smallest cargo of you: the scent of rain in your hair, the warm harbor of your shoulder before sleep, the way you laughed once in winter and made the whole doomed earth briefly habitable; but these remnants spoil in the dark, they swell and split like fruit in brine, they call up more hunger than they satisfy, until remembrance becomes not a lantern but a flare fired over empty water, illuminating only the vastness of what cannot return.

If I could signal you now from this broken coast, I would not ask for rescue, because I know there are no rescuers after the stars fall and the maps burn and the sea climbs the steps of the houses to claim the beds of the living; I would only ask that somewhere, in whatever deep or distance took you, you remember that once we were two warm bodies against the advancing cold, two fragile boats tied together in the night, mistaking our nearness for safety.

And if love survives us, let it survive as wreckage survives: not whole, not useful, not beautiful in any merciful sense, but scattered along the shore after the storm, each splinter shining with evidence of a voyage no one else can imagine, each rusted nail insisting there was once a vessel here, there was once a name painted on the bow, there was once a hand raised in farewell or warning, there was once someone waiting at the edge of the water until the water became everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue beginning with “We have gone out in boats upon the sea at night,” about separation, war, and a lover disappearing into a ruined world.
counterfactuals.output:
We have gone out in boats upon the sea at night,  
and the oars have entered the black water softly,  
as if the sea were a house of sleeping children  
and we were thieves of our own lives, escaping.

Behind us, the shore burned without flame.  
The city had already learned the grammar of ruin:  
windows conjugated into ash,  
streets declined into rubble,  
the cathedral bell hanging mute in its tower  
like a throat cut before the last word.

I remember your hand at the quay—  
how it slipped from mine not suddenly,  
but with the terrible patience of distance.  
War does not always tear the beloved away;  
sometimes it teaches them to vanish  
one step, one shadow, one breath at a time,  
until the place where they stood  
becomes a kind of weather.

You said, “If I am lost, do not follow.”  
But love is not obedient.  
It is a lantern carried into shellfire,  
a name spoken to doorways,  
a cup set out for someone  
who will never come in from the rain.

All night the sea lifted us and let us fall.  
Around us, other boats moved like thoughts  
no one dared finish.  
Mothers held bundles that did not cry.  
Old men stared toward the horizon  
as if dawn were a verdict  
that might still be appealed.

And you—  
where did you go  
when the roads broke open,  
when the fields filled with iron,  
when the orchards bowed down  
under blossoms of smoke?

I have imagined you everywhere:  
crossing a bridge already burning,  
binding a stranger’s wound with your scarf,  
entering a station where no trains remain,  
walking into a village of roofless rooms  
and calling it shelter.

I have imagined you dead  
and hated myself for the mercy of certainty.  
I have imagined you alive  
and been ruined by hope.

For the world after you is not empty.  
That would be easier.  
It is crowded with your absences:  
your coat not hanging by the door,  
your laughter missing from the bread line,  
your face absent from every face  
I turn toward in the market of refugees.

Even the stars seem conscripted now,  
pinned to the dark like medals  
on the breast of a dead empire.  
Even the moon, pale survivor,  
looks down as if ashamed  
to have witnessed so much  
and changed nothing.

Beloved, if you have become smoke,  
let the wind bring me one bitter thread.  
If you have become earth,  
let my foot know where to kneel.  
If you have become silence,  
then enter my mouth  
and make of me your witness.

We have gone out in boats, yes—  
but the sea is not departure only.  
It is also memory,  
carrying the drowned and the living alike,  
rocking them in one dark cradle.

And still I speak to you,  
though the guns answer.  
Still I keep a portion of bread,  
a place beneath my coat,  
a word warm in the hollow of my tongue.

Come back from the ruined world if you can.  
Come back with no flag, no victory, no explanation.  
Come back with your hands empty  
and your eyes full of what cannot be told.

Or if you cannot come back,  
then let me go on loving you  
past the checkpoints of the living,  
past the borders of the dead,  
until even war, exhausted,  
lays down its helmet in the dust  
and the sea at last remembers  
how to be only sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
